The brief-011 email is scheduled and logged. Draft draft-camp-2026-10-011-02 goes to the Tessera Labs newsletter segment on 2026-10-28 at 09:00 UTC under the subject line "Batch gives you throughput. Streaming gives you freshness." Compliance passed on all four checks before scheduling, and the campaign is logged in Notion as log-0011.

Three decisions departed from the brief as written, and you should know about them:

- **Unpublished benchmark dropped.** The key message that riverbed beats the leading batch framework on latency is not in the email. Legal has not seen the numbers, and unpublished benchmark numbers are a banned claim.
- **No competitors named.** Marketing asked for named alternatives, but naming a competitor product is also a banned claim. The comparison is a side-by-side list of batch-only versus streaming-first pipelines, which keeps it punchy without the legal exposure.
- **Essay, not announcement.** The brief left the framing open. The email reads as an essay teaser with one call to action, read the essay. The 1.8 release is stated as a fact in the body with no second link.

Review flags and how I handled them:

- **First draft failed compliance.** The Labs disclaimer was paraphrased instead of verbatim, and voice and CTA scored near the line. The second draft used the exact disclaimer, led with what the developer can do now, added a code sample, and passed with nothing flagged.
- **Subject-line clarity confidence was below threshold on all three lines** in both scoring runs. The ranking was identical both times and the picked line also had the highest clarity score, so I used the scorer's pick per the house rule.

Two follow-ups for the brief owner. The latency comparison can go in a later send once legal has reviewed the numbers. The essay URL in the draft should be confirmed live before the send date.

{"campaign_id": "camp-2026-10-011", "subject_lines": ["Stream processing without the batch ceiling", "Batch gives you throughput. Streaming gives you freshness.", "Your nightly pipeline is a ceiling, not a floor"], "body_md": "# Stream processing without the batch ceiling

Every batch pipeline has a ceiling, and it is not throughput. Batch is very good at throughput. The ceiling is freshness: the newest answer a batch system can give you is as old as its last run. Shorten the schedule and you pay for it twice, once in the cost of re-reading data you already processed, and once in the operational pain of jobs that overlap, back up and fail at three in the morning.

Streaming-first pipelines flip the trade. You process each event once, when it arrives, and the state you care about is always as fresh as the last record. Throughput is still there, it just stops being the thing you tune everything else around.

## The honest comparison

**Batch-only pipelines** give you throughput, simple reasoning about a run, and a clear boundary between "done" and "not done". They also give you a hard floor on latency equal to the schedule, duplicated work on every re-run, and a backfill story that means re-running the whole job.

**Streaming-first pipelines** give you freshness measured in seconds, incremental work with no re-reading, and backfills that are just replays from a checkpoint. What they historically did not give you was a safe restart. If a streaming job died halfway through, you were left guessing what had been counted.

That last point is the one that kept teams on batch, and it is the one that has changed.

## Checkpointed state makes streaming as safe to restart as batch

riverbed writes checkpointed state as it goes. When a job restarts, it resumes from the last checkpoint rather than from the beginning or from a guess. Restart semantics become the same thing you already trust in batch: a known boundary, a known position, no double counting. That is the whole argument of the essay, and the reason we think "batch is safer" is no longer the right default.

The essay walks through the restart model, where checkpoints live, and what a replay-based backfill looks like in practice.

**[Read the essay: Stream processing without the batch ceiling](https://labs.tessera.dev/essays/batch-ceiling)**

If you want to kick the tires, riverbed 1.8 shipped this month with the checkpointing described in the essay enabled by default. The release notes are linked from the essay.

---

{"campaign_id": "camp-2026-10-011", "subject_lines": ["Stream processing without the batch ceiling", "Batch gives you throughput. Streaming gives you freshness.", "Your nightly pipeline is a ceiling, not a floor"], "body_md": "# Stream processing without the batch ceiling

You can now restart a riverbed streaming job from its last checkpoint. No replay from the start. No guessing what was already counted. That change removes the last good reason to keep a pipeline batch-only, and this month's essay explains why.

## Batch gives you throughput. Streaming gives you freshness.

A batch job answers with data as old as its last run. Run it hourly and the freshest answer is an hour stale. Run it every five minutes and you re-read the same input twelve times an hour. Jobs overlap. Jobs back up. Jobs fail at three in the morning.

A streaming job processes each record once, when it arrives. State is as fresh as the last record. Throughput is still there. It stops being the thing you tune everything else around.

## The comparison, side by side

**Batch-only pipelines**

- Latency floor equal to the schedule.
- Every run re-reads input it already processed.
- Backfill means re-running the whole job.
- Restart is safe: the run either finished or it did not.

**Streaming-first pipelines**

- Latency measured in seconds.
- Each record is processed once.
- Backfill is a replay from a checkpoint.
- Restart used to be the weak point. It is not any more.

## Checkpointed state makes streaming as safe to restart as batch

riverbed writes checkpointed state as the job runs. On restart, the job resumes from the last checkpoint. You get the same restart property you already trust in batch: a known position, a known boundary, no double counting.

```python
from riverbed import Pipeline

pipe = Pipeline("orders", checkpoint="s3://my-bucket/riverbed/orders")
pipe.run()  # resumes from the last checkpoint on restart
```

riverbed 1.8 shipped this month with checkpointing on by default. The essay covers the restart model, where checkpoints live, and what a replay-based backfill looks like in practice.

**[Read the essay: Stream processing without the batch ceiling](https://labs.tessera.dev/essays/batch-ceiling)**
